passages.t: Why do the wicked live on?
passages.happening:
‘Then Job answered’ (verse 1). “Listen carefully to my words; let this be your consolation to me. Bear with me while I speak; then, after I have spoken, you may go on mocking” (verses 2-3). “Look at me and be appalled; put your hand over your mouth” (verse 5).

Then he asks the question: “Why do the wicked live on, growing old and increasing in power?” (verse 7). Their children grow up around them. Their homes are safe, and no rod from God touches them. Their herds breed without fail. Their little ones skip about, singing to tambourine and lyre. ‘They spend their days in prosperity and go down to Sheol in peace’ (verse 13).

And all the while they say to God, “Leave us alone! For we have no desire to know Your ways” (verse 14). Yet Job will not join them: ‘their prosperity is not in their own hands, so I stay far from the counsel of the wicked’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
This chapter closes the second round. Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar have each painted the downfall of the wicked, and each portrait was aimed at Job. Here, for the first time, Job takes on their doctrine as a claim about the world and tests it against what anyone can see. It is his most direct rebuttal in the book.

His picture of the prosperous wicked is everything an ancient household hoped for: children growing up around them, safe homes, herds that calve without loss, and children dancing to the lyre, the tambourine and the pipe. To go down to Sheol in peace was the ideal death, quick and untroubled at the end of a full life. Job answers Zophar's portrait in chapter 20 almost point for point.

Notice verse 16. Job does not envy the wicked or take their side. He says their prosperity is not in their own hands, and he keeps away from their counsel. His complaint is not that he wants to be like them. It is that the friends' account of the world is not true.
passages.later: A psalm says what Job saw: ‘Behold, these are the wicked’, ‘always carefree as they increase their wealth’ (Psalm 73:12).
passages.hard:
Is Job right that the wicked prosper and God does nothing?

Job's observation is true to experience, and it is confirmed elsewhere in Scripture, which is why the book lets it stand. Psalm 73, Jeremiah 12 and Ecclesiastes all describe the same thing. The friends' position, that the wicked are always visibly punished in this life, is the one the book rejects (42:7).

At the same time, Job speaks in anguish and at the edge of his argument. He does not claim that God never judges, only that the pattern the friends describe does not hold. Interpreters answer his challenge in several ways. Some stress that the Old Testament points slowly toward judgment and life beyond death, Daniel 12:2 most clearly, which changes the terms of the question. Others stress that the book of Job gives no theoretical answer at all: God's speeches in chapters 38 to 41 call Job to trust a wisdom larger than any formula. Many Christian readers hold both. The prosperity of the wicked is real, final justice is still ahead, and in the meantime faith waits.
passages.asks: Job looked honestly at a world that did not fit his friends' teaching. Ask whether you have ever ignored something true because it did not fit what you were taught. And ask how you hold on to God when the world does not make sense.

passages.t: How often is the lamp put out?
passages.happening:
“How often is the lamp of the wicked put out? Does disaster come upon them?” (verse 17). Are they blown away like straw and chaff?

“It is said that God lays up one’s punishment for his children. Let God repay the man himself, so he will know it” (verse 19). What does a dead man care about his household after him?

“Can anyone teach knowledge to God, since He judges those on high?” (verse 22). One man dies full of strength, secure and at ease. Another dies in bitterness, never having tasted good. ‘But together they lie down in the dust, and worms cover them both’ (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Job's question in verse 17 picks up Bildad's picture of the lamp of the wicked going out (18:5-6). How often, he asks, does that actually happen?

Verse 19 quotes a common saying, that God stores up a man's punishment for his children. Job rejects it. Punishment that falls on someone's children is no justice to the man himself.

Verses 23 to 26 set two men side by side, one full of vigor, one bitter, and both are covered by the same worms. Death levels the prosperous and the miserable alike. It is the observation of Ecclesiastes too.
passages.later: Ecclesiastes saw the same: “In my futile life I have seen both of these: A righteous man perishing in his righteousness, and a wicked man living long in his wickedness” (Ecclesiastes 7:15).
passages.asks: Job would not accept a saying just because it was often repeated. Ask what sayings about suffering you have repeated without testing. And ask what it means for you that death comes alike to the strong and the bitter.

passages.happening:
“Behold, I know your thoughts full well, the schemes by which you would wrong me” (verse 27). The friends ask where the house of the great man is now, and the tents of the wicked.

“Have you never asked those who travel the roads? Do you not accept their reports?” (verse 29). The evil man is spared in the day of calamity. No one denounces him to his face. He is carried to his grave in honor, a watch is kept over his tomb, the earth lies sweet on him, and crowds follow behind.

“So how can you comfort me with empty words? For your answers remain full of falsehood” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Job appeals to something every ancient reader could check: the reports of travelers, who moved along the trade routes and brought back news of many lands. Their testimony, he says, is that the evil man is often spared and buried with honor.

The funeral of verses 32 and 33, a crowd following the bier and a watch kept over the tomb, was the honor given to a great man.

The chapter ends where it began. Job asked for consolation in verse 2, and the friends have offered empty words, hevel, the breath or vapor of Ecclesiastes. The friends came to comfort him (2:11). This is what their comfort has come to.
passages.asks: Job called his friends' comfort empty. Ask whether your comfort has ever been more about defending your own beliefs than about the person in front of you. And ask what comfort that is not empty would sound like.
